clue.text: A charitable gift almost beats the blues

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of it, so the final letter of the gift is dropped

parts.note: a dole is a charitable handout
drums beat, and beats on them are drums

explanation.surface: A generous donation nearly drives away someone's sadness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beats' reads as a verb in the surface but is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the doldrums is an idiom for low spirits, a state of gloom or depression.

clue.text: To deem unsatisfactory and deprive of rank

indicators.note: unsatisfactory means not in proper order, so these letters must be put into a different order

parts.note: the letters of both words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An officer judged inadequate and stripped of rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unsatisfactory' looks like what the officer is deemed to be; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To demote is to reduce someone to a lower grade or rank, as in the army or a company.

clue.text: Cat crossing a river by airway

indicators.note: crossing means spanning something, so the cat word stretches across the other pieces placed inside it

parts.note: a lynx is a wild cat
taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A wild cat crosses a river near an airway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' reads as near; it is a link meaning the answer is given by what comes before. LYNX splits after its first letter to hold A and R.
explanation.definitionFit: The larynx, or voice box, is the part of the throat that the air passes through on its way to the lungs.

clue.text: Advice once given to conceal gold bar in coat

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so the old word for advice wraps around the other piece

parts.note: rede is an archaic word for advice; once flags it as old
an ingot is a bar of cast metal, especially gold

explanation.surface: Old advice: hide a gold bar in your coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advice once given' sounds like counsel offered in the past; it is a pointer to rede, an obsolete word for advice.
explanation.definitionFit: A redingote is a long double-breasted coat, originally a riding coat, the name taken from the English word.

clue.text: Be in earnest in ignoble company

definitions.meaning: first meaning: be serious about doing something
second meaning, read literally: a stingy or base commercial firm

explanation.surface: Be serious, even if you mix with low people.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the phrase word by word: mean as base or ungenerous, business as a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to be fully serious about one's intentions, while read literally it describes a base or miserly firm.

clue.text: Assurance displayed by father returning to see doctor

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word for father is read backwards

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
lo is an old exclamation meaning look or see
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A father shows confidence as he goes back to visit the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Aplomb is calm self-confidence and poise, which is what assurance means as a personal quality.

clue.text: Capital husband withdraws from part of diocese

indicators.note: withdraws from means leaves, so the letter for husband is taken out of the district word

parts.note: a diocese is divided into parishes
H is the standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A married man in a big city pulls out of his church parish.
explanation.definitionFit: Paris is the capital city of France, so it is one example of a capital.

clue.text: Like Pepusch's version of Gay's beggarly play

definitions.text: Like Pepusch's version of Gay's beggarly play

parts.note: surface reading: a play by John Gay about beggars
setter's reading: Pepusch arranged the music for Gay's ballad work about a beggar, so his version is sung on stage

explanation.surface: A description of a composer's treatment of John Gay's play about beggars.
explanation.walkthrough: John Gay wrote The Beggar's Opera (1728), and the German-born composer Johann Christoph Pepusch arranged its music.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to or resembling opera, and Pepusch's arrangement turned Gay's play into a sung musical drama.

clue.text: Rallying, make bed again

indicators.note: to make the words is to build something new from them, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of both words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Recovering from illness, someone makes the bed once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rallying' looks like recovering; here it is the noun from rally, to tease.
explanation.definitionFit: To rally someone is an old sense of tease, so rallying is playful mocking talk, the same as banter.

clue.text: The Circle Line, where there's always a Pole at the terminus

definitions.text: The Circle Line, where there's always a Pole at the terminus

parts.note: surface reading: the London Underground line that runs in a loop

parts.words: where there's always a Pole at the terminus
parts.note: setter's reading: a great circle on the globe whose two ends are the North and South Poles

explanation.surface: A joke about the London Underground's Circle Line always having a Polish person at the end of the line.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes Pole look like a Polish passenger; it is a geographic pole, where every line of longitude ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A meridian is a line of longitude, half of a great circle on the globe running from one geographic pole to the other.

clue.text: Society member as backer of Covent Garden, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a member of the Religious Society of ..., a Quaker
second meaning: a supporter enrolled in an arts patrons' scheme such as the ... of Covent Garden

explanation.surface: A club member is also a supporter of the Royal Opera House.
explanation.walkthrough: Covent Garden here is the Royal Opera House in London, whose donors' scheme is called the Friends of Covent Garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Quakers call themselves Friends, and arts institutions call their paying supporters Friends, so one word serves both.

clue.text: Settles among contents of this transporter?

definitions.text: Settles among contents of this transporter?

parts.note: surface reading: someone settles down among the cargo
setter's reading: settles are wooden benches with high backs, the kind of furniture this vehicle carries

explanation.surface: Someone makes themselves comfortable among the cargo of a lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settles' reads as a verb; it is the plural of settle, a high-backed bench. A pantechnicon is a large removal van.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantechnicon is a large van for moving house, carrying furniture such as settles.

clue.text: Half Lord Alfred's inner circle can be found in this joint

indicators.note: inner says this piece goes on the inside of the other
half means only the first of the two equal parts of the poet's surname is kept

parts.note: Alfred, Lord Tennyson, the Victorian Poet Laureate
a circle is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Half of Tennyson's close friends can be found at this get-together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inner circle' looks like one phrase meaning a clique; split it, and circle is the letter that goes inside the first half of TENNYSON.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenon is the projecting tongue of wood that fits into a mortise, forming a carpentry joint.

clue.text: Seafaring type with a chair on board

definitions.text: Seafaring type with a chair on board

parts.words: Seafaring type with a chair on board
parts.note: surface reading: a sailor who has brought a piece of furniture onto the ship
setter's reading: the ship's officer has a sling seat named after him, a plank hung from a rope for working over the side

explanation.surface: A sailor who has brought his own seat aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' seems to mean aboard ship, but the chair is literally a board: the seat named after this petty officer is a plank on ropes.
explanation.definitionFit: The bosun is the ship's officer in charge of rigging and deck crew, and a bosun's chair is named after him.

clue.text: Arabs, possibly, involved in this shrewd bargaining?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, cryptic: Arabs are a breed of horse, so a deal involving them is literally trading in horses
second meaning: hard-headed negotiation with give and take on both sides

explanation.surface: Arab traders might be engaged in this kind of hard-nosed haggling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arabs' seems to mean people from the Arab world; here it is the breed of horse, and 'possibly' flags it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse-trading is the idiom for tough negotiation with mutual concessions, from the reputation of dealers selling horses.

clue.text: She produced a law for a Roman and Egyptian god

parts.note: taken as written
lex is the Latin word for law
taken as written
Ra is the ancient Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: A woman drew up a law that served both a Roman and an Egyptian deity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is the whole definition: the answer is a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandra is a woman's given name, so it can stand for she, an unnamed woman.

clue.text: One abandoning a cause after being immured by a goddess

indicators.note: being immured is being walled up, so this piece is shut inside the following ones

parts.note: Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and folly
post is the Latin for after, as in postwar
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deserter of a movement is walled up by an angry goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' looks like 'following'; it gives the prefix POST, which goes between A and the goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostate is someone who renounces their religion or principles, deserting a cause they once held.

clue.text: Risk including article in which sovereign appears

indicators.note: including means taking something in, so the risk word holds the article

parts.note: to imperil is to put at risk
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A dangerous piece of writing that features the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Risk' and 'article' look like nouns; risk is the verb and the article is grammatical.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperial describes an empire or emperor, holding supreme authority, which is the adjectival sense of sovereign.

clue.text: Persistent questioner given money for bread

parts.note: one who pumps someone for information
a nickel is an American five-cent coin

explanation.surface: A nosy interrogator is paid cash in exchange for some bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money for bread' looks like buying a loaf, or slang bread meaning cash; bread is just the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pumpernickel is a dense dark German rye loaf, a particular kind of bread.

clue.text: Way the old cross a main road, causing obstruction

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

indicators.note: to cross something is to stretch over it, so the old word straddles the road

parts.note: ye is an old spelling of the
the M1 is Britain's main motorway north from London, its 1 read as I

explanation.surface: Elderly people crossing a busy road hold up the traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Yorkshire; crosswords often read its digit as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: In old golf, a stymie was a ball blocking an opponent's line to the hole, so the word means an obstacle or hindrance.

clue.text: Tribe's head man is devious

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only the opening letter of the word for a people is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of tribe
Ricky is a man's name

explanation.surface: The chief of a tribe is a cunning man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head man' looks like one phrase for the chief; split it, and man is just a boy's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tricky is crafty and deceitful, full of tricks, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: A writer set out to get meat without one

indicators.note: set out can mean laid out afresh, so these three letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the meat word loses a letter

parts.note: venison is deer meat
one is the Roman numeral I, the letter removed

explanation.surface: An author sets off to buy meat but goes without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' reads as one phrasal verb meaning departed; it splits into the word set and its anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island and Kidnapped, is a famous Scottish novelist.

clue.text: Possibly the old style community spirit

indicators.note: possibly says the letters could be arranged some other way

parts.note: taken as written
OS stands for Old Style, the dating of the Julian calendar

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned ways may be what a community's character is made of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old style' reads as dated fashion; it is the abbreviation OS used for Julian calendar dates.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the characteristic spirit or guiding beliefs of a group, culture or institution.

clue.text: In real terms, change is not so pronounced

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

parts.note: the end of real runs into the start of terms

explanation.surface: In real terms, the change is less marked than it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail warns that the word which sounds like the answer, the church altar, is not the one meant; only the spelling hidden in the clue counts.
explanation.definitionFit: To alter something is to change or modify it, so the verb is a direct synonym.

clue.text: To dismount is safe, though both sides are missing

indicators.note: both sides means left and right, and missing says those two letters are taken away

parts.note: all right means safe and unhurt

explanation.surface: Getting off a horse is safe, even if you have no flanks to grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both sides' looks like the two ends of the word, but here it means the letters L (left) and R (right), each removed once.
explanation.definitionFit: To alight is to get down from a horse or vehicle, which is exactly what dismounting means.

clue.text: Fellow lacking experience of practical affairs

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a university fellow, a scholar teaching at a college
second meaning: theoretical and unworldly, of no practical relevance

explanation.surface: A man who has never had to deal with the real world.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one description of an unworldly man; 'Fellow' is a separate meaning, the college post.
explanation.definitionFit: A college fellow is a scholar, and the adjective describes ideas or people remote from real-world concerns.

clue.text: Join up and attend if directions are sent to the front

indicators.text: if directions are sent to the front
indicators.note: directions here are compass points, and sent to the front says the closing pair of compass letters moves to the start

parts.note: to attend is to pay attention, to listen

explanation.surface: Instructions for joining the army: sign up, and turn up when orders call you to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's directions are military orders and the front a battle line; E and N are compass points, which end the word for attend and move to its start.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlist is to sign up for the armed forces, which is the military sense of join up.

clue.text: A lodging-place in Cambridgeshire shire, naturally

parts.note: an inn is a place to stay the night
in and at both say where something is
Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
padding: an OCR repeat of the end of the county name, contributing no letters

explanation.surface: An inn somewhere in the English county of Cambridgeshire, described as natural.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambridgeshire is an English county in the east; the clue uses it to point to one of its towns, the cathedral city of Ely.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done innately comes from inborn qualities, by nature, which is what naturally means here.
